name: Italian Cuisine: From Pasta to Tradition
description: Start with dried pasta done properly, then the sauces, fresh pasta by hand, risotto and a pizza from a cold rise.

skills.name: The Cooking Water Is an Ingredient
skills.description: The starch the pasta leaves in the water is what makes a sauce cling. You keep a cup of it before draining, always.

skills.name: Finishing Pasta in the Pan
skills.description: Pasta drained a minute early and finished in the pan with the sauce and its own water, instead of sauce poured over a plate of pasta.

skills.name: Pasta Types
skills.description: Know which pasta shape for which sauce: long for oil, tube for chunky.

skills.name: Water & Flour Ratio
skills.description: The hydration of pasta dough: too wet is sticky, too dry won't bind.

skills.name: Kneading Pasta
skills.description: Develop gluten without overworking: smooth, supple dough.

skills.name: Rolling Pasta
skills.description: Thin, even sheets without tearing: the sign of skill.

skills.name: Sauce Reduction
skills.description: Low heat, time, and patience: concentrate flavour without burning.

skills.name: Balancing Acidity
skills.description: Tomato sauce needs fat and time to soften the acid bite.

skills.name: Carbonara Emulsion
skills.description: Eggs and cheese as a sauce: the science of not scrambling.

skills.name: Ragù Braising
skills.description: Long, slow cooking of meat and tomato: the soul of Bolognese.

skills.name: Constant Stirring
skills.description: Risotto demands attention: stir slowly, listen to the rhythm.

skills.name: Mantecatura Finish
skills.description: Cold butter into hot rice: creates the creamy wave.

skills.name: Risotto Doneness
skills.description: All dente, flowing but not soupy: the edge between two states.

skills.name: Bread Fermentation
skills.description: Time and temperature: the rise that builds flavour.

skills.name: Gluten Development
skills.description: Stretch and fold: build structure without overworking.

skills.description: High heat and steam: the final rise before the crust sets.

skills.name: Puffy Crust
skills.description: The edge that should char and puff: technique and heat.

lessons.title: The Cooking Water Is an Ingredient
lessons.description: The cloudy water you have been pouring down the sink is the only thing that makes a sauce stick to pasta.

preparationSteps.title: Salt the water properly, and nothing else
preparationSteps.description: Enough salt that the water tastes seasoned. No oil in the water — it coats the pasta and then the sauce slides off.

preparationSteps.title: Keep a mug of the water before you drain
preparationSteps.description: Put a mug in the sink and fill it from the pot before draining. Once the water is gone, it is gone, and there is no substitute.

preparationSteps.title: It is starch, which is why it thickens
preparationSteps.description: The pasta sheds starch as it cooks. That starch is an emulsifier: it binds oil and water into something that coats, instead of two things that separate.

questions.prompt: You drained the pasta, tipped all the water away, and your olive-oil sauce is sitting in a puddle at the bottom of the bowl. What was missing?
options: A little of the starchy cooking water, to bind the oil into a sauce
You should have cooked the pasta longer
questions.correctAnswer: A little of the starchy cooking water, to bind the oil into a sauce
questions.explanation: Oil and water separate on their own. The starch from the pasta is what holds them together, which is why a spoon of the cooking water turns oil into a sauce that coats.
questions.explainWrong: More oil gives you a bigger puddle, and butter is a different dish. Cooking the pasta longer only makes it soft — it does nothing about a sauce that will not cling.

questions.prompt: Should you add olive oil to the pasta cooking water to stop it sticking?
options: No — it coats the pasta and the sauce then slides off
Only if the pot is small
questions.correctAnswer: No — it coats the pasta and the sauce then slides off
questions.explanation: Oil floats and coats the strands as you drain, leaving them slippery. Pasta does not stick if there is enough water and you stir it in the first minute.
questions.explainWrong: It is a common habit, but it works against the whole point of the next step: sauce needs a surface it can grip. Stirring early and using enough water is what stops sticking.

lessons.title: Pasta Finishes in the Pan, Not on the Plate
lessons.description: The difference between home pasta and restaurant pasta is thirty seconds in the pan, not a better sauce.

preparationSteps.title: Drain it a minute early
preparationSteps.description: Take the pasta out while it is still slightly firmer than you want to eat it. It finishes cooking in the pan.

preparationSteps.title: Pasta into the sauce, never sauce onto the pasta
preparationSteps.description: The sauce is in a wide pan on the heat; the pasta goes in there. Sauce spooned over a plate only ever touches the top.

preparationSteps.title: Water in, and keep it moving
preparationSteps.description: A splash of the cooking water, and toss or stir hard for half a minute. It looks too wet and then suddenly turns glossy — that is the sauce forming.

preparationSteps.title: Cheese and fresh herbs off the heat
preparationSteps.description: Once it is glossy, off the heat. Cheese added over a flame goes stringy and splits out of the sauce.

questions.prompt: Why drain the pasta a minute before it is done?
options: Because it finishes cooking in the pan with the sauce
questions.correctAnswer: Because it finishes cooking in the pan with the sauce
questions.explanation: That last minute in the pan is where the pasta absorbs sauce instead of water. Drained fully cooked, it goes past al dente while you are tossing it.
questions.explainWrong: It is not about gas, and it is not meant to stay crunchy — it finishes to exactly al dente in the pan, which is the point. Draining it done and then heating it again is how pasta gets soft.

questions.prompt: Your pasta and sauce look wet and loose in the pan after tossing for ten seconds. What do you do?
options: Keep it moving on the heat for another twenty or thirty seconds until it turns glossy
questions.correctAnswer: Keep it moving on the heat for another twenty or thirty seconds until it turns glossy
questions.explanation: It always looks too wet just before it comes together. The starch and the fat emulsify with movement and heat, and then it visibly tightens and shines.
questions.explainWrong: Adding sauce makes it wetter, draining pours away the starch that is about to do the work, and flour is not how an Italian sauce thickens. It needs a few more seconds of agitation.

lessons.title: Tomato Sauce from Three Things
lessons.description: Tomato, garlic, olive oil. That's it. Learn why this is enough.

preparationSteps.title: Slice garlic thin
preparationSteps.description: Not minced — thin slices so you can fish them out later if you want.

preparationSteps.title: Gentle heat, oil, garlic
preparationSteps.description: Low heat, don't let it brown. You want sweet, not bitter.

preparationSteps.title: Add tomatoes
preparationSteps.description: Crush them in by hand. Bring to a bubble, not a boil.

preparationSteps.title: Time and salt
preparationSteps.description: 20 minutes minimum. Salt at the end, not before.

questions.prompt: Your garlic is turning brown in the oil. What went wrong?
questions.correctAnswer: The heat is too high
questions.explanation: Garlic burns at high heat. Low heat until the tomatoes go in, then keep it at a bubble.
questions.explainWrong: Old garlic and cheap oil do not brown on their own — heat does. Turn the flame down before you change anything else, or the next clove burns exactly the same way.

questions.prompt: After 20 minutes, the sauce tastes too acidic. How do you fix it?
options: Cook it longer with a lid off
questions.correctAnswer: Cook it longer with a lid off
questions.explanation: Time reduces acidity. Fat (butter, cream, or good oil) rounds it out too.
questions.explainWrong: Sugar leaves the sauce tasting sweet instead of ripe, and salt sharpens acidity rather than softening it. Fat does round the edge, but it is the uncovered simmer that actually drives the sharpness off.

lessons.title: Ragù Is Time, Not Technique
lessons.description: A ragù asks for three hours and almost no skill. What ruins it is heat, not inexperience.

preparationSteps.title: Brown the meat properly, in batches
preparationSteps.description: Colour is flavour, and crowded mince steams grey instead of browning. Two batches in a hot pan beats one full one.

preparationSteps.title: Soffritto slowly, before anything else goes in
preparationSteps.description: Onion, carrot and celery, finely chopped, softened gently for ten minutes. Rushed, they stay raw-tasting through three hours of cooking.

preparationSteps.title: A bare simmer for three hours, lid ajar
preparationSteps.description: Barely a bubble. A rolling boil tightens the meat and it stays tough no matter how long you give it.

preparationSteps.title: Milk near the end, and taste before salting
preparationSteps.description: A little milk softens the acidity and the texture. The pot concentrates as it reduces, so the salt goes in at the end, not at the start.

questions.prompt: Your ragù simmered for three hours and the meat is still tough and grainy. What went wrong?
options: It was boiling rather than simmering, which tightens the meat
questions.correctAnswer: It was boiling rather than simmering, which tightens the meat
questions.explanation: A braise softens meat by holding it just below a boil for hours. At a rolling boil the proteins tighten and squeeze out water, and no amount of extra time reverses that.
questions.explainWrong: Lean meat and too much tomato make a ragù drier and sharper, but neither makes it grainy — and more hours at a boil only makes it worse. The heat is the whole answer.

questions.prompt: When does the salt go in?
options: At the start, with the soffritto
Near the end, once it has reduced
Half at the start, half at the end
It does not matter in a long braise
questions.correctAnswer: Near the end, once it has reduced
questions.explanation: Three hours of reducing concentrates whatever salt is in the pot. Seasoned at the start, a ragù that tasted right at hour one is inedible at hour three.
questions.explainWrong: It matters more in a long braise than anywhere else, precisely because the liquid halves. Salting early — even half of it — is how a good ragù ends up too salty to serve.

units.title: Carbonara: The Emulsion
units.subtitle: Egg, fat and starch held together by nothing but heat and timing

lessons.title: Carbonara: The Science
lessons.description: Eggs and cheese as sauce, without cream. Learn the temperature window.

preparationSteps.title: Dice the guanciale
preparationSteps.description: Small cubes, render them gently so the fat releases.

preparationSteps.title: Beat eggs with cheese
preparationSteps.description: Not cooking them — just mixing until you have a glossy paste.

preparationSteps.title: Cook pasta
preparationSteps.description: Al dente. Reserve a cup of starchy water.

preparationSteps.title: The trick: temperature control
preparationSteps.description: Drain pasta, toss with fat from guanciale, then add egg mix off heat while stirring fast.

questions.prompt: Your carbonara scrambled. What happened?
options: The pan was too hot when you added the egg mix
questions.correctAnswer: The pan was too hot when you added the egg mix
questions.explanation: Off heat, stirring fast, splash of pasta water to cool it down. Those three things prevent scrambling.
questions.explainWrong: Egg age and guanciale change the flavour, not the texture. Scrambling is heat: the pan was still cooking when the egg went in. Off the heat, moving fast, with a splash of pasta water — that is what keeps it a sauce.

questions.prompt: The sauce is too thick, coating the pasta like glue. Fix it?
options: Splash of pasta water and stir
questions.correctAnswer: Splash of pasta water and stir
questions.explanation: Starch in the water loosens it. Cream is not traditional and breaks the emulsion.
questions.explainWrong: More egg thickens what is already too thick, and more cooking sets it harder. Cream is the tempting fix and the one that breaks it — starchy water loosens an emulsion without washing out the flavour.

lessons.title: Which Pasta, Which Sauce
lessons.description: Learn why every shape exists and which sauce it was born for.

preparationSteps.title: Understand Long Pasta
preparationSteps.description: Spaghetti, linguine, fettuccine: for oil-based, light, or cream sauces.

preparationSteps.title: Understand Tube Pasta
preparationSteps.description: Rigatoni, penne, fusilli: trap chunky sauces inside.

preparationSteps.title: Understand Filled Pasta
preparationSteps.description: Ravioli, tortellini: the filling is the sauce.

questions.prompt: You have a chunky Bolognese sauce. Which pasta shape holds it best?
questions.correctAnswer: Rigatoni
questions.explanation: Tubes trap the chunky sauce inside. Oil-based sauces need thin, long strands.
questions.explainWrong: Long thin strands let a chunky ragù slide straight off onto the plate. The meat ends up at the bottom of the bowl and the pasta comes up bare — the shape has nowhere to hold it.

questions.prompt: A creamy sauce with seafood: which long pasta?
questions.correctAnswer: Fettuccine
questions.explanation: Flat ribbons hold cream better than round strands.
questions.explainWrong: Round strands shed a cream sauce as fast as you lift them. A flat ribbon gives the sauce a surface to sit on, which is why cream is almost always served on ribbons.

questions.prompt: Pesto is best served with?
questions.correctAnswer: Linguine
questions.explanation: Pesto clings to flat pasta. Hand-rolled (trofie) also works beautifully.
questions.explainWrong: Penne and ravioli give pesto nowhere to cling — it slides off and pools at the bottom. Trofie is the Ligurian classic and works beautifully too, but of these the flat strand is the one that carries pesto best.

lessons.title: Dough: Water, Flour, Hands
lessons.description: Learn the ratio that binds: not too wet, not too dry.

preparationSteps.title: Pile the Flour
preparationSteps.description: Mound it on a clean bench, not in a bowl. You need room to work.

preparationSteps.title: Make a Well
preparationSteps.description: Poke a hole in the top, add eggs and a pinch of salt.

preparationSteps.title: Bring It Together
preparationSteps.description: Use a fork to break the yolks and beat them, then start drawing in flour.

preparationSteps.title: When It Gets Thick
preparationSteps.description: Use your hands. It's sticky now — that's normal.

preparationSteps.title: Knead
preparationSteps.description: Push away with the heel of your hand, fold back, turn 45°, repeat. 8-10 minutes.

questions.prompt: Your dough is cracking at the edges. What do you do?
options: Add a tiny drop of water
questions.correctAnswer: Add a tiny drop of water
questions.explanation: Cracks mean too little hydration. A single drop on each crack, then knead.
questions.explainWrong: Adding flour or kneading harder makes it worse: cracking is a dry dough asking for water, and both answers take water away or force a dough that has none to give. Starting over throws out a dough that is one drop from right.

questions.prompt: After 5 minutes of kneading, your dough is still sticky. Normal?
options: Yes, keep going, it'll smooth out
questions.correctAnswer: Yes, keep going, it'll smooth out
questions.explanation: Sticky dough becomes smooth with kneading. Don't add flour — you'll dry it out.
questions.explainWrong: Adding flour now is the reflex that ruins fresh pasta. Sticky at five minutes is the gluten still forming; flour at that moment gives you a dough that rolls stiff and cooks tough, and you cannot take it back out.

questions.prompt: Order the steps of making pasta dough from scratch
items: Pile flour and make a well
Beat eggs into the well with a fork
Start drawing flour into the egg
Use hands when it gets too thick
questions.explanation: This is the order that builds structure without tearing or drying.
questions.explainWrong: Beating the eggs before the well is built sends them across the counter. And kneading before the flour is drawn in leaves dry pockets that never hydrate — resting cannot fix what the mixing skipped.
correctOrder: Pile flour and make a well
Beat eggs into the well with a fork
Start drawing flour into the egg
Use hands when it gets too thick

lessons.title: Rolling Thin
lessons.description: The feel of thin, even dough: paper-thin but not torn.

preparationSteps.title: Start in the Middle
preparationSteps.description: Place the ball in the centre of the bench. Work from your body outward.

preparationSteps.title: Press, Don't Roll
preparationSteps.description: Use the heel of your hand, pressing outward in a spiral. Rotate after each press.

preparationSteps.title: Let It Rest
preparationSteps.description: Every 2-3 minutes, let it rest for a minute. Gluten relaxes.

preparationSteps.title: Watch the Thickness
preparationSteps.description: You should see your hand shadow through it.

preparationSteps.title: Cut and Dry
preparationSteps.description: Cut into sheets, lay on a drying rack for 10-15 minutes before cooking.

questions.prompt: Is this pasta sheet ready for cutting?
questions.correctAnswer: Yes, it's thin enough
questions.explanation: You can see hand shadows through it — that's the right thickness.
questions.explainWrong: Calling a sheet too thick when the light already passes through means you keep rolling until it tears. The shadow test is the whole point: once you can see through it, stop.

questions.prompt: Your dough tears as you press it. What happened?
options: It wasn't rested long enough between presses
The flour on top burned it
questions.correctAnswer: It wasn't rested long enough between presses
questions.explanation: Gluten needs to relax. If you press continuously, it fights back and tears.
questions.explainWrong: Pressing harder or blaming the water reads the tear backwards. A rested dough stretches; an unrested one springs back and splits along the line you just pushed. The fix is time, not force.

lessons.title: Risotto Fundamentals
lessons.description: The technique that demands attention: constant stirring, hot stock, rice that gives off starch.

preparationSteps.title: Stock hot
preparationSteps.description: The stock must be simmering in a pot beside you. Cold stock stops the cooking.

preparationSteps.title: Toast the rice
preparationSteps.description: Dice the onion, sauté gently, add rice. Toast for 1 minute until the rice moves freely.

preparationSteps.title: Wine first
preparationSteps.description: A splash of wine, let it absorb. You're sealing the rice, not cooking it yet.

preparationSteps.title: Add stock in waves
preparationSteps.description: One ladle at a time. Only when the liquid is almost absorbed do you add the next.

preparationSteps.title: Keep stirring
preparationSteps.description: Slow circles, don't break the rice. You're listening and watching, not timing.

preparationSteps.title: Mantecatura
preparationSteps.description: At the end, off heat: cold butter and cheese folded in. Creates the flow.

questions.prompt: How do you know when to add the next ladle of stock?
options: When the rice looks dry on top
When the previous liquid is almost absorbed
When the rice grains show white
questions.correctAnswer: When the previous liquid is almost absorbed
questions.explanation: Not bone dry, not swimming. Almost absorbed. That's the rhythm of risotto.
questions.explainWrong: A timer ignores how fast your pan runs, and waiting for dry rice means the grains stick and catch. Almost absorbed is the point where the rice still has something to work with.

questions.prompt: Your risotto is soupy after 18 minutes. What happens next?
options: Add the butter and cheese now
Cook it longer without adding stock
questions.correctAnswer: Cook it longer without adding stock
questions.explanation: Time varies. If it's still soupy at 18 minutes, keep stirring until the rice is creamy and coats the spoon.
questions.explainWrong: Stopping early leaves raw rice in a soup, and more stock makes more soup. Finishing with butter and cheese onto a loose risotto just thins them. Let the liquid go before you finish it.

lessons.title: Pizza Dough Basics
lessons.description: The foundation: hydration, fermentation, salt timing.

preparationSteps.title: Mix the dough
preparationSteps.description: Flour, water, yeast. Mix until no dry flour remains. Rest 30 minutes.

preparationSteps.title: Add salt and oil
preparationSteps.description: After 30 minutes, add salt and oil. Knead 5 minutes until incorporated.

preparationSteps.title: Bulk fermentation
preparationSteps.description: 4-8 hours at room temperature. Fold every hour for the first 3 hours.

questions.prompt: Why do you add salt and oil after 30 minutes, not at the start?
options: Salt kills yeast if added too early
questions.correctAnswer: Salt kills yeast if added too early
questions.explanation: Salt directly on dry yeast can kill it. After hydration, it's safe.
questions.explainWrong: Oil slows gluten a little but does not stop it, and tradition is never the reason in bread. Salt straight onto dry yeast draws the water out of it, and a dough that never rises will not tell you why.

lessons.title: Gluten, Rise and the Puffy Edge
lessons.description: You are not kneading this dough into shape — time does that. What you control is the oven and how you handle the edge.

preparationSteps.title: Time builds the gluten, not your arms
preparationSteps.description: A wet dough left alone develops strength by itself. A few folds twenty minutes apart do more than ten minutes of kneading, which is why this is the easiest dough to start with.

preparationSteps.title: The cold rise is doing the work
preparationSteps.description: A night in the fridge gives the flavour and the structure. It is also forgiving: an hour more or less changes nothing.

preparationSteps.title: Never touch the last two centimetres
preparationSteps.description: Press and stretch from the centre outwards and leave the rim alone. The gas trapped in that rim is the whole cornicione — rolled with a pin, it is gone.

preparationSteps.title: Hottest oven, and preheat the tray
preparationSteps.description: As hot as your oven goes, with the tray or a pan already scorching inside it. Pizza needs a blast of heat from below in the first minute or it dries out instead of puffing.

questions.prompt: Your pizza came out flat, with no raised edge. You rolled the dough out with a rolling pin. What happened?
options: The pin pushed out the gas in the rim, which is what puffs into the crust
questions.correctAnswer: The pin pushed out the gas in the rim, which is what puffs into the crust
questions.explanation: The cornicione is made of bubbles the long rise put there. A rolling pin flattens them out of the dough, and nothing in the oven can put them back.
questions.explainWrong: A hot oven is what you want, and more yeast gives a yeastier flavour rather than a better rim. Too much sauce makes the middle soggy, but it is the pin that removed the edge.

questions.prompt: You put the pizza on a cold tray into a preheated oven. Why is the base pale and dry?
options: The cold tray had to heat up first, so the base never got its blast of heat
questions.correctAnswer: The cold tray had to heat up first, so the base never got its blast of heat
questions.explanation: A pizza base cooks from below in the first minute. A cold tray spends that minute warming up, so the base dries out slowly instead of blistering.
questions.explainWrong: An underproved dough would be dense rather than pale and dry, oil is not what browns a base, and the oven being hot is exactly what you need — it just has to be hot in the metal under the dough, not only in the air.

questions.prompt: This dough gets a few folds instead of ten minutes of kneading. Why does that work?
options: It does not — kneading is always better
A wet dough left to rest develops gluten on its own; the folds just line it up
It only works with strong flour
questions.correctAnswer: A wet dough left to rest develops gluten on its own; the folds just line it up
questions.explanation: Gluten forms when flour is hydrated and given time. Folding organises the structure that resting already built, which is why a long cold rise beats hard kneading for pizza.
questions.explainWrong: Kneading is one route, not the only one, and the air in the dough comes from fermentation rather than from folding. Strong flour helps but the resting does the work either way.

missions.title: Aglio, olio e peperoncino
missions.summary: Four ingredients and no sauce to make: the dish that teaches you what the cooking water is for.

steps.title: Salted water on, and nothing else in it
steps.description: Plenty of water, salted until it tastes seasoned. No oil. Put the spaghetti in and stir for the first minute so it does not stick.

rescues.answer: No coarse salt? Fine salt works, just use less than it looks like you need.
Sticking together? Stir now — it only happens in the first minute.

steps.title: Garlic gently in the oil while the pasta cooks
steps.description: Sliced garlic and chilli into cold oil in a wide pan, over low heat. Low, slowly, until the garlic is pale gold and smells sweet. Brown garlic is bitter and there is no way back.

rescues.answer: Garlic gone brown? Start the oil and garlic again — bitter garlic ruins a four-ingredient dish.
No fresh chilli or flakes? Black pepper is a different dish but a good one.
Garlic colouring too fast? Pan off the heat for a moment; the oil carries on cooking it.

steps.title: Keep a mug of the water, then drain a minute early
steps.description: Fill a mug from the pot before you drain. Take the spaghetti out while it is still slightly firm — it has another minute to go in the pan.

rescues.answer: Firmer than you would want to eat it, and a full mug of cloudy water saved.
Already poured the water away? Hot water with a spoon of the pasta's own starch is a poor substitute — next time, mug in the sink first.

steps.title: Pasta into the pan, water in, and keep it moving
steps.description: Spaghetti into the garlic oil with a good splash of the cooking water. Toss or stir hard over medium heat. It looks too wet, then turns glossy and coats every strand — that is when it is done.

rescues.answer: Glossy and clinging to the strands, no oil pooling at the bottom of the pan.
Still not coming together? Another splash of water and keep moving — it needs agitation, not more oil.
Too dry and clumping? A little more of the cooking water loosens it straight away.

steps.title: Off the heat, parsley, eat it now
steps.description: Heat off, chopped parsley through it, and to the table. This dish waits for nobody — it tightens and dulls as it sits.

rescues.answer: Still glossy on the plate, garlic pale gold and sweet rather than brown and bitter.
No parsley? It is optional; the dish is the garlic, the oil and the water.

missions.title: Ragù Bolognese
missions.summary: Slow, low heat: meat, tomato, and time create depth. The engine of Italian cooking.

steps.title: Soffritto
steps.description: Dice the pancetta, onion, carrot, celery (the holy trinity). Render pancetta, then sweat the vegetables gently until soft.

rescues.answer: No celery? Just onion and carrot. No carrot? Onion and celery. One at least.

steps.title: Meat
steps.description: Add ground meat. Stir to break it up. It should turn grey then slightly brown, but not crispy.

rescues.answer: Dark brown means too much heat. The ragù will taste burnt later. Lower the heat.

steps.title: Wine
steps.description: Splash of white wine. Let it bubble away — this adds acidity and depth.

rescues.answer: No wine? A splash of water, but wine is better.

steps.title: Tomato and milk
steps.description: Add crushed tomatoes and a splash of milk. The milk softens the acidity. Low heat from here on.

rescues.answer: Smells burnt? Too much heat. Move the pan to a quieter part of the stove or use a diffuser.
Slow bubble, oil rising to the surface, flavours deepening.

steps.title: Wait
steps.description: 45 minutes minimum, 2 hours is better. Stir now and then. Taste after 45 — if flat, keep going.

rescues.answer: Dark, complex, sweet, rich. If watery, simmer uncovered to reduce.

steps.title: Season and finish
steps.description: Salt to taste. Serve over fresh pasta or dried. A little grated Parmesan on top.

rescues.answer: Tastes flat? Salt. Tastes bitter? A splash of milk and simmer 5 more minutes.

missions.title: The sauce that isn't cooked
missions.summary: No cream, no pan on the heat at the end. The sauce is egg, cheese and pasta water, held together by the warmth already in the bowl.

steps.title: Salt the water
steps.description: A big pot, well salted — the guanciale and the pecorino are salty, so taste the water and stop short of the usual.

rescues.answer: It should taste seasoned but not like the sea. The cheese brings the rest.

steps.title: Render the guanciale
steps.description: Cold pan, no oil, low heat. Let the fat come out slowly until the pieces are golden and crisp at the edges. Keep every drop of the fat.

rescues.answer: Dark and hard means it went too fast. Low and slow is what renders fat instead of burning it — start again if it tastes bitter.
No guanciale? Pancetta is the close cousin. Smoked bacon changes the dish but teaches the same emulsion.
Golden pieces sitting in a pool of clear fat.

steps.title: Beat the eggs and cheese
steps.description: Eggs, the extra yolk, the pecorino and a lot of black pepper, beaten to a thick paste. Do this while the pasta cooks, not after it drains.

rescues.answer: Thick enough to fall off the fork in a ribbon. Runny means it needs more cheese.
Clumping on the fork is the cheese grated too coarse. Grate it finer and it melts instead of seizing.

steps.title: Off the heat, then the egg
steps.description: Drain, saving a mug of the water. Pasta into the guanciale pan off the heat, wait thirty seconds, then the egg mix and a splash of water, stirring hard the whole time.

rescues.answer: Scrambled means the pan was still cooking. There is no saving it — but next time let the pan stand half a minute before the egg goes in.
Thick and claggy: another splash of pasta water and keep stirring. The starch is what loosens it without washing out the flavour.
It coats each strand and still slides on the plate. Glossy, not set — if it holds its shape, it went too far.

missions.title: Your First Fresh Pasta
missions.summary: From dough to plate: make, roll, dry, cook and eat your own pasta.

steps.title: Make the dough
steps.description: Follow the lesson: flour well, eggs, fork, hands, knead 8-10 minutes.

rescues.answer: Too crumbly? One drop of water. Too sticky? Work it longer before adding flour.
Smooth, elastic, not sticky. Wrap and rest 30 minutes.

steps.title: Rest the dough
steps.description: 30 minutes wrapped in plastic. This lets gluten relax.

rescues.answer: You can't over-rest it at room temperature.

steps.title: Roll it out
steps.description: Press, spiral, rotate. Let it rest 1 minute every 2-3 presses. Aim for thin enough to see your hand.

rescues.answer: If it tears, let it rest and try again from a thicker part. You can patch.
Even thickness, translucent, no holes.

steps.title: Cut and dry
steps.description: Cut into ribbons (tagliatelle), lay on a clean towel or drying rack. 15 minutes before cooking.

rescues.answer: Not drying? It'll stick in the pot. 15 minutes is the minimum.

steps.title: Cook in salted water
steps.description: Boiling, salted water. Fresh pasta takes 2-3 minutes only.

rescues.answer: As soon as it floats and stays up, it's done. Taste one strand.
It's sinking and cooking unevenly? The water might not be boiling hard enough.

steps.title: Finish with butter and cheese
steps.description: Reserve pasta water. Drain, toss with cold butter, grated Parmesan, splash of pasta water.

rescues.answer: No Parmesan? Use any hard cheese you have. Pecorino is traditional.
Silky, coating the pasta, no grease pooling.

missions.title: Risotto, by the spoon
missions.summary: Twenty minutes at the pan without walking away. It is the one dish where the stirring is the technique, not a chore.

steps.title: Stock on, and keep it hot
steps.description: The stock simmers in its own pan next to you the whole time. Cold stock into hot rice stops the cooking dead each time you ladle.

rescues.answer: No stock? Hot salted water with a bay leaf is honest and works. Never use cold water.
It should be steaming and barely trembling, not at a rolling boil.

steps.title: Soffritto
steps.description: Onion in oil over low heat until soft and translucent — no colour. Five to seven minutes.

rescues.answer: Brown onion gives the risotto a harsh edge you cannot remove. Lower the heat and add a spoon of stock to cool the pan.
Soft, glassy, and it smells sweet rather than sharp.

steps.title: Toast the rice
steps.description: Rice in dry, stir for two minutes until the grains are hot and the edges go translucent with a white dot at the centre. Then the wine, and let it disappear.

rescues.answer: Sticking means the pan is too hot with too little fat. Keep the grains moving.
Pick a grain out: a clear rim around a white centre means it is toasted.

steps.title: Ladle and stir
steps.description: One ladle of stock, stir, wait until it is almost absorbed, repeat. Eighteen minutes or so. Almost absorbed — not dry, not swimming.

rescues.answer: Catching on the base means you let it go too dry between ladles. Next ladle a little sooner.
Out of stock before the rice is done? Hot water finishes it. Better that than stopping early.
Taste a grain from eighteen minutes on: tender with the faintest resistance at the core, and no chalk.

steps.title: Mantecatura
steps.description: Off the heat. Cold butter and the parmesan, beaten in hard for a minute. This is what turns cooked rice into risotto.

rescues.answer: Stiff and heavy: a splash of hot stock and keep beating. It should move, not stand.
Shake the pan — the risotto should settle in a slow wave. That is all'onda, and it is the test.

missions.title: Pizza from a cold rise
missions.summary: Almost all of it is waiting. Twenty minutes of work, a long rise, and the hottest oven you own.

steps.title: Flour, water, yeast
steps.description: Mix flour, water and yeast to a shaggy mass. No salt, no oil yet. Leave it 30 minutes so the flour drinks properly.

rescues.answer: It is meant to be wet and untidy at this point. Wet your hands instead of adding flour.
Ready to rest when there is no dry flour left in the bowl.

steps.title: Now the salt and oil
steps.description: Work the salt and oil in. Salt on dry yeast at the start draws the water out of it and the dough never rises.

rescues.answer: It gets slacker before it gets stronger. Fold it over on itself rather than kneading hard.
Worked in when you cannot feel grains of salt between your fingers.

steps.title: Fold, then let it rise
steps.description: Four folds, 20 minutes apart. Then cover and leave it: 6 to 8 hours at room temperature, or overnight in the fridge.

rescues.answer: Risen when it has roughly doubled and the surface is domed with bubbles underneath.
Short on time? A warmer spot speeds it up, but the flavour comes from the long slow rise.

steps.title: Shape it by hand
steps.description: Press from the centre outwards, leaving the last two centimetres untouched. That rim is the cornicione. Never use a rolling pin.

rescues.answer: Sticking to the counter means not enough semolina underneath. Dust, do not add flour to the dough.
Tearing means it is under-rested. Cover it and give it ten minutes, then try again.
Stretched enough when you can see light through the middle.

steps.title: Hottest oven you have
steps.description: Oven as high as it goes with a tray or stone preheated inside for 30 minutes. Sauce thin, cheese sparse. Six to ten minutes.

rescues.answer: Burnt base with a pale top: the stone was too hot and too low. Move it up a shelf.
Stuck to the peel or tray? Too much sauce, or it sat too long before going in. Build it fast and launch it.
Done when the rim is blistered and spotted brown and the base lifts stiff off the tray.
